title: The Empty Corner of the Station
passage:
At a small train station near Haru's town, there was an empty corner beside the ticket gate. People usually walked past it without noticing. One winter, the town asked local students to suggest ways to use the space. Some students wanted vending machines, while others suggested a large advertisement board. Haru's group proposed something different: a small waiting area with local information and a bench. Their idea came from watching older passengers who sometimes stood near the wall while waiting for rides. The group first measured the space and counted how many people passed through the station at different times of day. They found that the station was busiest in the morning, but the corner was most useful in the afternoon, when people waited longer for buses or family members. The students also interviewed passengers. Some wanted a place to sit, while visitors said they often had trouble finding information about nearby parks, shops, and walking routes. The town liked the proposal but explained that the budget was limited. The students therefore changed their plan. Instead of buying a new digital display, they designed a simple wooden information board that volunteers could update. A local carpenter offered leftover wood, and an art club painted a map. The town paid only for a strong bench and weather-resistant materials. After the waiting area opened, Haru's group returned to observe it. They noticed that the bench was used often, but the map was sometimes blocked by people standing nearby. The students moved one sign and added a small arrow on the floor. They also found that tourists asked the same three questions repeatedly, so they added answers directly to the board. Haru had imagined that good design meant having a clever idea at the beginning. The project taught him something else. A useful place is created through observation, testing, and small corrections. The first plan does not need to be perfect if people are willing to watch how it is actually used. Months later, the station manager told the students that passengers had begun leaving notes with suggestions for new local information. The empty corner had become more than a place to wait; it had become a small connection between the station and the town.

The town later asked the students to review the corner after six months. They found that local information changed more often than expected. One shop had closed, a new walking event had started, and the bus timetable had changed. Because volunteers could replace paper notices easily, the simple board adapted better than a fixed digital design would have. Haru realized that low-cost solutions can sometimes be stronger because they are easier to maintain. The group added a monthly check so old information would not remain on display. They also left one small empty section for temporary notices. By then, Haru no longer judged the project by how modern it looked. He judged it by whether people could understand, update, and continue using it without special help.
translation:
春の町の小さな駅には、改札の横に誰も気に留めない空きスペースがありました。冬に町が活用案を募集し、自動販売機や広告板などの案が出る中、春のグループは地元情報を置いた小さな待合スペースを提案しました。高齢の乗客が迎えを待ちながら壁際に立っている姿を見たことがきっかけでした。生徒たちはまず場所を測り、時間帯ごとの通行人数を調べました。朝が最も混雑する一方、午後にはバスや家族を待つ人が長く滞在することが分かりました。利用者への聞き取りでは、座る場所が欲しいという声と、観光客から近くの公園や店、散歩道の情報が分かりにくいという声が出ました。予算が限られていたため、新しいデジタル表示ではなく、ボランティアが更新できる木製案内板に変更しました。地元の大工が余った木材を提供し、美術部が地図を描き、町は丈夫なベンチなど最低限の費用だけを負担しました。完成後に観察すると、ベンチはよく使われるものの地図が人に隠れる問題が見つかり、看板の位置や床の矢印を調整しました。また観光客が同じ質問を繰り返すため、その答えも案内板に加えました。春は良いデザインとは最初から賢い案を出すことだと思っていましたが、観察し、試し、少しずつ直すことが大切だと学びました。数か月後には利用者自身が新しい地元情報の提案を残すようになり、空きスペースは単なる待合場所ではなく、駅と町をつなぐ場所になっていました。

町は半年後、生徒たちにその場所を再点検してもらいました。店の閉店、新しい散歩イベント、バス時刻の変更など、地域情報は予想以上に変化していました。紙の案内板はボランティアが簡単に更新できるため、固定的なデジタル表示より柔軟でした。春は、現代的に見えることより、誰でも理解し、更新し、特別な助けなしに使い続けられることの方が重要だと考えるようになりました。
